title: Hot Keys
subtitle: Solving single-shard bottlenecks in distributed caches when a single celebrity or viral event generates 500k+ reads/sec.
keyTakeaways: Sharding a cache horizontally provides cluster throughput, but any individual key hashes to exactly one Redis master node.

Because Redis processes commands sequentially on a single core, an extreme hot key (200k+ RPS) saturates that single shard's CPU and network interface, causing timeouts for all unrelated keys on the same node.
Mitigate hot keys using short-TTL in-process L1 caches in application memory or by salting keys across multiple cluster hash slots.

sections.heading: The Single-Shard Saturation Trap
sections.body: Horizontal scaling solves uniform data distribution, not skewed access patterns. In Redis Cluster, CRC16 hashing assigns each key to one of 16,384 slots mapped across master nodes. When a celebrity tweet, flash-sale SKU, or emergency notification goes viral, traffic doesn't spread across your cluster. It funnels into a single thread on a single machine. Once that thread caps out at 100% CPU, latency spikes, and every other key assigned to that shard begins timing out.
bullets: Hot Key Detection: Use client-side probabilistic sketches (such as Count-Min Sketch in an Envoy proxy or client SDK) or Redis's native `redis-cli --hotkeys` to detect keys exceeding safe traffic thresholds (e.g., >5,000 RPS).

L1 In-Process Memory Cache: Place a high-speed local LRU cache (e.g. Caffeine or Go Ristretto) inside application pods with a 1–2 second TTL. If you run 80 application pods, an L1 cache absorbs 98% of reads in local RAM with zero network round trips.

Key Salting (Replication Across Shards): Append a pseudo-random suffix (`item:42#shard_{0..15}`) when writing the key. Writers update all 16 replicas, and readers query a random salt shard, spreading 400,000 RPS across 16 different Redis cluster nodes.

sections.heading: Trade-offs in Key Salting and Invalidation Coordination
sections.body: Key salting scales read throughput linearly with the number of shards, but it introduces operational costs on the write and invalidation paths.
bullets: Write & Invalidation Amplification: Salting across 16 shards means every write or `DEL` must execute 16 separate network calls. Salting should only be activated for dynamically identified hot keys, never for the entire keyspace.

Avoid Hash Tag Trap in Redis Cluster: In Redis Cluster, any text inside curly braces `{...}` forces keys into the same hash slot. Writing `{item:42}#1` through `{item:42}#16` would defeat the purpose entirely by routing all 16 copies to the same physical node!

Redis Client-Side Caching (RESP3): Using Redis 6+ tracking mode, the server proactively broadcasts invalidation messages to connected application nodes whenever tracked keys change, keeping L1 memory in sync without aggressive polling.

tradeOffs.option: Tiered L1 In-Process Cache (App RAM) + L2 Redis
tradeOffs.pros: Zero network hops; read throughput scales directly with the number of stateless application pods.
tradeOffs.cons: Consumes application heap memory and introduces a brief staleness window unless using RESP3 invalidation broadcasts.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Celebrity profiles, trending hashtags, flash-sale catalogs, and global feature toggles.

tradeOffs.pros: Spreads CPU and network load across the Redis Cluster without increasing application memory footprint.
tradeOffs.cons: Multiplies write operations and invalidation fan-out by N.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large cached blobs or counters queried by thousands of ephemeral serverless functions without local disk/memory continuity.

interviewTip: During high-scale system design interviews, bring up the single-shard hot key bottleneck unprompted, and explain how an in-process L1 cache (1–2s TTL) prevents single-thread CPU starvation.
